P1.name: Treating the percentage number as a quantity with the original units
P1.example: Calling 25% of £80 “£25”, or adding £25 for a 25% increase. Calculate 25/100 of £80 = £20.

P2.name: Converting a percentage to a decimal/fraction with the wrong place value

P3.name: Confusing the percentage change amount with the new total
P3.example: For a 25% increase on £80, correctly find £20 but give £20 as the new price. Add it to £80 to obtain £100. Using 0.25 instead of 1.25 as a multiplier for the new price is the same conceptual family.

P4.name: Applying a change in the wrong direction
P4.example: A 25% decrease on £80 gives £100. Subtract £20 to obtain £60; use 0.75 rather than 1.25 if using a multiplier.

P5.name: Using the new amount as the denominator for percentage change
P5.example: For £80 → £100, calculate 20/100 × 100 = 20%. Compare with the original £80: 25%.

P6.name: Using the whole new amount instead of the difference in the numerator
P6.example: For £80 → £100, calculate 100/80 × 100 and call 125% the increase. £100 is 125% of the original, so the increase is 25%.

P7.name: Inverting the fraction for percentage change
P7.example: For £80 → £100, use 80/20 × 100 = 400%. The change goes over the original: 20/80 × 100.

P8.name: Failing to convert a proportion to a percentage
P8.example: Correctly calculate 20/80 = 0.25, then label the increase 0.25%. Multiply by 100 to obtain 25%.
